Doctor: hi , mrs . vance . it's good to see you again . how have things been since our last visit ?
Patient: oh , hello doctor . well , i ... i'm a bit rattled , to be honest . i've been having some trouble with my eyes .
Doctor: i'm sorry to hear that . can you tell me more about what's going on ?
Patient: it's just ... everything has started looking all fuzzy . like i'm looking through a dirty window , you know ? and then , uh , a few days ago i started seeing these little black dots , just floating around in front of me . it's making me really nervous .
Doctor: okay . how long has the fuzziness been going on for ?
Patient: i think it's been a few months , slowly getting worse . but the dots ... those just started about a week ago .
Doctor: i see . and is it in both eyes or just one ?
Patient: both , i think . it's just ... everything is just not sharp anymore .
Doctor: okay . now , i know we've been working on your diabetes . have you been able to keep up with your metformin and your diet ?
Patient: i've been trying , really . but it's been hard lately . my daughter , sarah , she moved down to florida last month , and she was the one who usually drove me to the pharmacy and helped me with the grocery shopping . now i'm having to rely on the bus , and ... well , the bus doesn't go nearly as far as she could drive . i've missed a couple of doses because i couldn't get to the store in time .
Doctor: i'm sorry to hear about the move , that's a big change . and how are you doing financially ? i know you're on a fixed income , is the cost of the medication becoming an issue ?
Patient: it's ... it's a bit tight , you know . i worry about the cost of new things . if you tell me i need some expensive eye drops or something , i don't know if i can ... i just don't know .
Doctor: we'll figure that out , don't you worry about that right now . we'll look for the most affordable options . now , besides the vision , have you noticed anything else ? any numbness in your hands or feet ?
Patient: oh , yes . my toes have been feeling all tingly , like they're falling asleep .
Doctor: okay . and any dizziness or headaches ?
Patient: no , nothing like that .
Doctor: any changes in how often you're going to the bathroom or feeling extra thirsty ?
Patient: well , i have been drinking a lot more water lately , but i figured that's just because of the heat .
Doctor: okay . let's take a look at you . i'm gon na check your vision first . go ahead and cover your left eye for me . read the bottom line on that chart there .
Patient: uh ... it's too fuzzy . i can only see the middle line . i can't make out the bottom one at all .
Doctor: okay . now the other eye .
Patient: same thing . it's just ... blurry .
Doctor: alright . let me take a look inside your eyes with the ophthalmoscope . just look straight ahead for me . okay . uh huh . yeah . okay , look over here . i'm seeing some small hemorrhages and some exudates in the retina . that's basically some leaking and bleeding in the back of the eye .
Patient: oh dear . is it bad ?
Doctor: it's something we need to address quickly . hey , dragon ? show me the last a1c . okay , your a1c was 9.2 percent three months ago , which is quite high . that explains a lot of this . when your blood sugar stays high for too long , it damages the tiny blood vessels in your eyes .
Patient: i just ... i didn't think it would affect my sight this fast .
Doctor: it can happen gradually and then you notice it all at once . so , here's the plan . i'm very concerned that this is diabetic retinopathy . i want you to see a specialist , an ophthalmologist , for a full dilated exam and to see if you need any treatment like laser therapy or injections .
Patient: will that be expensive ?
Doctor: we'll check with your insurance and see if there's a clinic that works on a sliding scale if needed . hey , dragon ? order a referral to ophthalmology for urgent evaluation of diabetic retinopathy . and for your diabetes , i want to adjust your medication to help bring that sugar down . i'm gon na increase your metformin dose . i'll send the prescription to the pharmacy , and since you're having trouble with transport , i'm gon na see if we can get your meds delivered to your house . would that help ?
Patient: oh , that would be a blessing . truly .
Doctor: okay . now , i want to be very clear about one thing . if you ever see a sudden "curtain" falling over your vision , or if you have a sudden increase in those floaters , or if you see flashes of light , i want you to go straight to the emergency room . don't wait for the bus , call an uber or a taxi , just get there immediately . do you understand ?
Patient: a curtain ... yes , i understand . go straight to the er .
Doctor: exactly . i'll have the nurse help you set up the delivery for your meds and give you the specialist's contact information .
Patient: thank you , doctor . i feel a bit better knowing what's going on .
Doctor: you're welcome . we'll get this sorted out . take care , mrs . vance .
Patient: you too . bye now .

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Vision changes.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Mrs. Eleanor Vance is a female patient who presents today with complaints of vision changes. She describes her vision as "fuzzy," comparing it to looking through a dirty window. She reports that this blurriness has been progressing over the last few months. Additionally, she reports the onset of "little black dots" floating in her vision starting approximately one week ago. These symptoms are bilateral.

The patient has a history of Type 2 Diabetes. She admits to missing several doses of metformin recently due to transportation barriers; her daughter, who previously provided transport to the pharmacy and grocery store, moved to Florida last month. The patient currently relies on the bus for transportation. She also expresses anxiety regarding her fixed income and the potential cost of new medications.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Neurological: Endorses tingling in her toes. Denies dizziness and headaches.
• Endocrine: Endorses increased thirst.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• Visual Acuity: Decreased bilaterally; patient was unable to read the bottom line of the visual acuity chart in either eye.
• Ophthalmoscopic Exam: Findings significant for small hemorrhages and exudates in the retina.

RESULTS

Last A1c (3 months ago) was 9.2%.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Mrs. Eleanor Vance is a female patient with Type 2 Diabetes presenting with bilateral blurred vision and floaters.

Diabetic Retinopathy.
• Medical Reasoning: The patient's symptoms, combined with an elevated A1c of 9.2% and physical exam findings of retinal hemorrhages and exudates, are highly suggestive of diabetic retinopathy.
• Medical Treatment: I have increased the patient's Metformin dosage to improve glycemic control. To address transportation barriers, I am arranging for medication home delivery.
• Additional Testing: I have ordered an urgent referral to an ophthalmologist for a full dilated examination and evaluation for potential laser therapy or injections.

Patient Agreements: The patient expressed relief and is in agreement with the plan.

INSTRUCTIONS

The patient was instructed to go immediately to the emergency room if she experiences any of the following: a sudden "curtain" falling over her vision, a sudden increase in floaters, or the appearance of flashes of light.

Doctor: alright , let's get started . sarah miller , date of birth 5 / 12 / 95 . mrn 4-4-2-1-0-9 . she's here for her six-week postpartum follow-up . hi sarah , it's good to see you again . how are things going at home with the little one ?

Doctor: hi elena, good to see you. what's been going on since the last time i saw you?

Doctor: okay, so you're describing hot flashes and chills. how long has this been happening?

Doctor: i can imagine that's very stressful. are you having these during the night as well?
Patient: yeah, the night sweats are the worst. i wake up and the sheets are literally soaked. i'm not sleeping more than four hours a night. and then there's this... brain fog. i'll be in the middle of a sentence and just... poof. the word is gone.
Doctor: brain fog, okay. and how has your mood been? any increased anxiety or irritability?
Patient: i'm a nightmare. my husband says i'm a different person. i just snap at everyone. it's probably because i'm so tired. and it's not just that, i'm also taking care of my mom now—she's got advanced dementia—so i'm basically working two full-time jobs. i don't have any time for myself.
Doctor: it sounds like you're under a tremendous amount of pressure right now. let's just double check a few other things. have you noticed any changes in your bladder? like, are you going to the bathroom more often than usual?
Patient: yeah, actually. i feel like i have to go every twenty minutes. i didn't think it was related, but maybe it is?
Doctor: it could be. and any other issues? any chest pain or shortness of breath?
Patient: no, nothing like that.
Doctor: okay. let's do a quick physical exam. i'll just start with your vitals. hey dragon, vitals are blood pressure one thirty-two over eighty-four, heart rate seventy-two. lungs are clear, heart sounds are normal. your thyroid doesn't feel enlarged. everything looks pretty standard on the physical side.
Patient: so... is this just part of getting older? i'm fifty-two, so i figure it's the change, right?
Doctor: it certainly sounds like you're in the menopausal transition. the symptoms you're describing—the hot flashes, night sweats, mood swings, and the urinary frequency—are all very common. now, we have a few options. we can try some non-hormonal things, like adjusting your sleep hygiene or using certain antidepressants for the flashes, or we can talk about hormone replacement therapy, which we call hrt.
Patient: i'm scared of the hormones. i read something online about cancer.
Doctor: that's a common concern. the risk depends on the type of hormones and your personal history. because you still have your uterus, if we do estrogen, we have to give you progesterone as well to protect the lining of the uterus. for most women, the benefit of getting their life back—sleeping again, focusing at work—outweighs the small increase in risk. 
Patient: i just want to be able to function again. i can't keep snapping at my kids and my husband.
Doctor: i understand. let's start with a low dose and see how you feel. i'm going to prescribe an estradiol patch, zero point zero five milligrams, which you'll put on once a week. and i'll give you progesterone, one hundred milligrams, to take by mouth every night. the progesterone actually helps with sleep, so that should help with the insomnia.
Patient: okay, once a week for the patch, and the pill every night.
Doctor: exactly. now, i want to run a few labs just to make sure everything else is on track. hey dragon, order an fsh level, an lh level, and a lipid panel.
Patient: okay. how long until i feel better?
Doctor: you should start noticing a difference in the hot flashes within a couple of weeks. but i want you to be aware of some safety things. if you notice any sudden, severe swelling in one of your legs, or if you have any sudden shortness of breath or chest pain, i want you to go to the emergency room immediately because those can be signs of a blood clot, which is a rare but serious side effect of hormones. 
Patient: oh wow. okay. emergency room for leg swelling or chest pain. got it.
Doctor: right. and i want to see you back here in six weeks to see if the dose is working or if we need to adjust it. does that sound like a plan?
Patient: yeah, that sounds good. thank you, doctor.
Doctor: you're welcome. we'll get those prescriptions sent over to your pharmacy now. bye.

Doctor: yes, just like that. okay, i see a mild resting tremor in the right hand, but it's definitely improved from last time. now, let me move your left arm for you. okay... yeah, there's some noticeable rigidity here in the elbow and wrist. and if you could just stand up and walk toward the door and back for me?

Patient: oh yes it is just... it's been getting so bad lately i can't even get into my car without a struggle my daughter sarah she has to practically lift me in and out of the seat and i just hate feeling like a burden you know
Doctor: i understand that can be very frustrating how long has this been going on for
Patient: um well it's been a few months i suppose but it really just started acting up about six weeks ago it's just this... this deep ache and sometimes it feels like my hip is just bone-on-bone if that makes any sense
Doctor: it does make sense you're describing a grinding sensation
Patient: exactly! and it clicks too sometimes i'll just be standing there and it goes click and i just... oh i'm so worried i'm going to need one of those metal hips i've seen on the news and i just don't know if my insurance will even cover the good kind of surgery
Doctor: we'll take it one step at a time and we'll see what the imaging shows first does the pain travel anywhere or is it just right there in the joint
Patient: it's mostly in the groin area and then it kind of shoots down the side of my leg but it doesn't go all the way to my knee usually
Doctor: okay and how is it in the morning
Patient: oh goodness i'm stiff as a board for the first hour i just have to shuffle around the kitchen until i loosen up
Doctor: i see any other symptoms we should know about any fever or chills lately
Patient: no nothing like that
Doctor: any numbness or tingling in your legs or feet
Patient: no no just the ache
Doctor: any back pain or trouble with your bladder or bowels
Patient: no the back is fine oh i forgot to tell you my granddaughter had her first ballet recital last weekend and she was just darling i wish you could have seen the little tutu she wore
Doctor: that sounds lovely mrs. gable but let's try to stay focused on your hip for a moment so i'm going to have you stand up for me and just walk a few steps toward the wall
Patient: okay here i go... oh just let me hold onto the chair for a second
Doctor: no problem just take your time alright as i'm looking at your gait you're definitely leaning a bit to the left to avoid putting weight on that right side let's do a quick exam here i'm going to move your leg
Patient: ow! right there
Doctor: okay so there's definitely some pain with internal rotation of the right hip and i can feel a bit of crepitus which is that crunching feeling you mentioned your strength in the leg seems fine though
Doctor: hey dragon i'm noting limited internal rotation of the right hip with associated pain and palpable crepitus
Patient: so what does that mean doc am i getting the surgery
Doctor: well i reviewed the x-rays you had done at the imaging center last week and they show some significant joint space narrowing and osteophytes in the right hip joint which basically means you have osteoarthritis
Patient: oh lord here it comes the surgery
Doctor: not necessarily mrs. gable we can try some conservative things first i don't want to jump straight to a hip replacement if we can avoid it i want to start you on some naproxen five hundred milligrams twice a day for the inflammation
Patient: will that make my stomach hurt i've had problems with those kinds of pills before
Doctor: i'll have you take it with a full meal to protect your stomach and we'll start with a low dose and see how you do also i want to get you into physical therapy to help with that stiffness
Patient: i don't know how i'll get there i don't drive anymore sarah takes me but she works full time during the week
Doctor: we can look for a therapist that has evening hours or maybe see if they offer some home exercises you can do with her on the weekends hey dragon order a referral for outpatient physical therapy for right hip osteoarthritis
Patient: okay i guess i can try that
Doctor: alright so we'll do the medication and the therapy and i want to see you back here in four weeks to see if the pain has improved if it hasn't we can talk about a cortisone injection into the joint but let's try the other things first do you have any other questions
Patient: no i think that's it i just hope this works
Doctor: i think it'll help get you moving a bit better it was good seeing you mrs. gable
Patient: you too doctor

Hip pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Mrs. Gable is a female patient who presents with right hip pain that has been present for several months and has worsened over the last six weeks. She describes the pain as a deep ache located in the groin area with occasional radiation down the lateral aspect of the leg. She reports "bone-on-bone" sensations and clicking in the joint. She notes significant morning stiffness lasting approximately one hour. The patient reports difficulty with transfers, specifically entering and exiting her vehicle, and requires assistance from her daughter. She expresses anxiety regarding the possibility of surgical intervention and concerns regarding insurance coverage. The patient's daughter provides her transportation as the patient no longer drives.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Constitutional: Denies fever and chills.
Musculoskeletal: Reports right hip pain and stiffness.
Neurological: Denies numbness or tingling in the lower extremities.
Genitourinary: Denies bladder or bowel issues.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Musculoskeletal
- Gait: Patient exhibits an antalgic gait, leaning to the left to offload the right hip.
- Right Hip: Pain upon internal rotation. Palpable crepitus noted. Strength is intact.

RESULTS

X-rays of the right hip reveal significant joint space narrowing and osteophytes.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Right hip osteoarthritis.
- Medical Treatment: Prescribed naproxen 500 mg twice daily for inflammation. Patient was instructed to take this medication with a full meal to avoid gastrointestinal upset.
- Specialist Referrals: Referral placed for outpatient physical therapy to address stiffness and joint function. Discussion held regarding scheduling conflicts due to the patient's reliance on her daughter for transportation.

The patient is instructed to follow up in 4 weeks to evaluate the effectiveness of the medication and physical therapy.

dialogue:
Doctor: hello mr. harrison, come on in. i see you're here for some pain in your side. can you tell me more about what's going on?
Patient: yeah, it's just... it's this stabbing thing, right here in my back and side. it comes and goes, but when it hits, man, i can't even stand up straight. it's been like two days of this.
Doctor: okay, so it's intermittent stabbing pain in your right flank. have you noticed any other symptoms, like maybe some changes when you go to the bathroom?
Patient: yeah, actually. i've been peeing blood. it's like a pinkish color, you know? and i feel like i gotta go every five minutes but then nothing really comes out.
Doctor: i see. have you had any fever, chills, or nausea?
Patient: no fever, i don't think. i mean, i feel like crap, but no shaking or anything. just the pain.
Doctor: alright. have you ever had something like this happen before?
Patient: no, never. i mean, i had a bad flu a few years back, but nothing like this. 
Doctor: okay. and what do you do for work, mr. harrison? i want to see how this is affecting your day-to-day.
Patient: i do framing, construction. it's all hourly pay, doc. that's the problem. i've already missed two days this week and my boss is already breathing down my neck about the timeline on the southside project. i can't afford to just sit around and wait for this to go away.
Doctor: i understand the stress of that. we'll try to get a plan together so you can get back to work safely. alright, let's do a quick exam. if you could just lean forward for me...
Patient: uh, okay. 
Doctor: i'm just going to tap on your back here. tell me if this hurts.
Patient: ow! yeah, right there. stop, stop.
Doctor: alright, i've got it. hey dragon, mark right-sided cvatenderness. okay, you can sit back up. so, i see you already had a ct scan done at the urgent care yesterday. let me pull that up.
Patient: yeah, they did the scan but they didn't really tell me what it was, just said it was a stone. how big is it? is it gonna pass?
Doctor: okay, looking at the images here... yes, it's a kidney stone. it's about 4 millimeters in size and it's currently lodged in your right ureter, which is the tube connecting the kidney to the bladder. the good news is that stones under 5 millimeters usually pass on their own.
Patient: 4 millimeters... that sounds small, but it feels like a knife. can't you just, i don't know, blast it out with a laser or something so i can go back to work tomorrow?
Doctor: for a 4 millimeter stone, we usually try a conservative approach first. surgery or lithotripsy is typically reserved for larger stones or if the pain becomes uncontrollable. the first step is to help the stone move along. i'm going to prescribe you something called tamsulosin. it's a medication that relaxes the muscles in your ureter to help the stone slide through.
Patient: okay, how do i take that?
Doctor: you'll take one 0.4 mg capsule once a day. i also want you to drink a ton of water—really push your fluids. and i want you to use a stone strainer, which is just a little mesh filter you put in the toilet. if you catch the stone, bring it into the office so we can analyze what it's made of.
Patient: and the pain? i can't frame a house if i'm doubled over.
Doctor: for the pain, you can use over-the-counter ibuprofen. take 600 mg every six to eight hours as needed. but i want to be very clear about when this becomes an emergency.
Patient: alright, i'm listening.
Doctor: if you develop a fever over 101.5 degrees, or if you find that you are completely unable to urinate at all, you need to go to the emergency room immediately. that could mean the stone is causing a total blockage or an infection, which is a serious situation. do you have a way to get to the er if that happens?
Patient: yeah, my wife is usually home, she can drive me. 
Doctor: okay, good. i'll send the prescription to your pharmacy now. i want to see you back here in two weeks to make sure the stone has passed. if it hasn't, we'll discuss other options.
Patient: two weeks. alright. i just hope this thing moves fast.
Doctor: i hope so too. any other questions?
Patient: no, i think that's it. thanks, doc.
Doctor: you're welcome. take care.

dialogue:
Doctor: good morning , mrs. harrison . it's nice to meet you . i'm dr. sterling .
Patient: nice to meet you too . sorry i'm a little late , the bus just ... it's just been a nightmare trying to get here with my daughter today .
Doctor: oh , no worries at all . i understand . so , i see here you're coming in because of some headaches ?
Patient: yeah . they've just been ... i don't know , it's like my brain is pulsing . it's not just a regular headache , you know ? it's like a hammering in my head , usually on the right side .
Doctor: okay . and how long has this been going on ?
Patient: i've had them since i was a teenager , really . but lately , they're just worse . like , way worse . i think it's the stress . i'm working the night shift at the warehouse right now , and trying to handle everything with my kid alone ... it's just a lot . i barely get any sleep before the bus comes .
Doctor: i'm sorry to hear that . it sounds like you have a lot on your plate . when these happen , do you notice anything else ? like , any nausea or maybe seeing things ?
Patient: oh , yeah . i get really sick to my stomach . and the weirdest thing is , i'll be looking at something and i just get these ... these blind spots . like little shimmering holes in my vision . and then the pain hits .
Doctor: okay . and when the pain is there , does light or sound bother you ?
Patient: god , yes . i have to go into a completely dark room and just lay there . if my daughter starts crying , it's like a knife in my head .
Doctor: mm-hmm . and what have you been taking for the pain ?
Patient: i've been using that excede-rin stuff , the migraine one . it helps a little bit if i catch it early , but mostly it just doesn't do anything anymore .
Doctor: okay . and how often are these happening now ?
Patient: um , i'd say maybe ...
Doctor: every week ?
Patient: no , not quite every week , but maybe twice a month ? and they last for , like , a whole day sometimes . i've missed two shifts at work this month already . i'm really worried about my job , especially with my insurance . i have a really high deductible , so i can't be spending a ton on fancy meds , but i can't keep missing work either .
Doctor: i hear you . we'll look for something that's effective but affordable . let's do a quick physical exam just to be safe . can you follow my finger with your eyes ? okay , great . pupils are equal and reacting well to light . i'm just going to check your strength here ... squeeze my hands . perfect . everything looks normal neurologically .
Patient: so it's not , like , a tumor or something ?
Doctor: based on your description of the blind spots , which we call an aura , and the way the pain behaves , this is very classic for migraine with aura . your exam is completely normal , so i'm not worried about anything more serious .
Patient: okay . that's a relief .
Doctor: so here is the plan . i want to give you something for when the attack starts . we'll try sumatriptan . it's a tablet , 50 milligrams . you take one as soon as you notice that shimmer in your vision or the pain starting .
Patient: is that expensive ?
Doctor: there is a generic version that is usually very cheap . hey dragon , order sumatriptan 50 mg , one tablet at onset of migraine , max two tablets in 24 hours .
Patient: okay .
Doctor: now , because you're working nights , i want you to try and keep a very strict sleep schedule , even on your days off . and make sure you're drinking plenty of water . i also want you to keep a headache diary . just write down when they happen and what you ate or did right before . that'll help us find your triggers .
Patient: i can try . it's hard with a toddler , but i'll try .
Doctor: i understand . now , one important thing . if you ever have a headache that comes on suddenly like a clap of thunder , or the worst headache of your life that feels different from these , i want you to go straight to the emergency room . do you understand ?
Patient: yeah , go to the ER if it's the worst one ever . got it .
Doctor: perfect . let's start with the sumatriptan and the diary , and i'll see you back here in six weeks to see if the frequency has gone down . any other questions ?

Migraine headache.

The patient reports associated symptoms including nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. She also describes experiencing "blind spots" or "shimmering holes" in her vision prior to the onset of the pain. She currently manages symptoms with Excedrin Migraine, which she reports is increasingly ineffective. Regarding social determinants of health, the patient is a single mother who works night shifts at a warehouse. She reports significant stress, poor sleep hygiene due to her work schedule, and transportation challenges via bus. She expressed concern regarding her high insurance deductible and the cost of medications, as well as the impact of these headaches on her employment.

• Neurological: Endorses pulsating right-sided headaches and visual disturbances (blind spots/shimmering).
• Gastrointestinal: Endorses nausea.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Neurological: Pupils are equal and reactive to light. Extraocular movements are intact. Upper extremity strength is normal in bilateral grips.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Migraine with aura.
• Medical Reasoning: The patient's symptoms of unilateral pulsating pain, nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, and preceding visual aura, combined with a normal neurological examination, are consistent with migraine with aura.
• Medical Treatment: Prescribed Sumatriptan 50 mg. The patient is to take one tablet at the onset of aura or pain, with a maximum of two tablets in a 24-hour period. I specified the use of a generic version to address the patient's financial concerns.

The patient was instructed to go to the emergency room immediately if she experiences a "thunderclap" headache or the worst headache of her life that differs from her usual migraine pattern. The patient will follow up in six weeks.

Patient: well, he had a bit of a cold, you know, just the usual runny nose and sneezing, maybe four or five days ago. then he started getting a fever. i mean, it wasn't super high, but he was warm to the touch. and then, uh, yesterday i noticed some kind of yellow gunk coming out of his right ear.

Doctor: i hear you, daycare policies can be a real struggle. so, just to be clear, the runny nose came first, then the fever, and then the ear pain and drainage?
Patient: yeah, that's right. 
Doctor: okay. now, is he on any medications right now? any tylenol or anything for the fever?
Patient: i gave him some children's tylenol last night, and it seemed to help him settle down a bit, but then he woke up again at 3 am screaming.
Doctor: alright. let's take a look at him. leo, can you be a big boy for me? let's see those ears. okay, i'm just going to use this little light. 
Doctor: hey dragon, open pediatric exam template. 
Doctor: alright, looking in the left ear... that looks perfectly clear. now the right ear... yeah, i see it. the eardrum is definitely bulging and it's very red, and there is some purulent drainage in the canal. okay, you can sit up now, leo. good job!
Patient: so it is an infection? is it bad? i'm a little worried because i'm not sure if our insurance is going to cover the expensive meds, and i really can't afford to miss another day of work this week since i'm hourly.
Doctor: it is a typical middle ear infection, what we call acute otitis media. it's very common. as for the medication, i'm going to prescribe a standard antibiotic that is usually very affordable and widely covered. i don't think we need any fancy expensive versions. hey dragon, order amoxicillin 400mg per 5ml, give 5ml twice daily for ten days. 
Patient: ten days? okay. do i just stop when he feels better?
Doctor: no, that's really important. you have to finish the entire bottle, even if he seems 100% better in three days. if you stop early, the infection can come back stronger.
Patient: okay, got it. finish the whole thing.
Doctor: exactly. now, keep giving him the tylenol for the pain and fever. if the fever doesn't go down within 48 hours of starting the antibiotic, or if you notice any swelling behind the ear or a very stiff neck, i want you to call me immediately or take him to the urgent care. 
Patient: okay, call you if the fever stays or if his neck gets stiff. 
Doctor: exactly. i'll have the nurse give you the printed instructions. do you have any other questions?
Patient: no, i think that's it. thank you, doctor.
Doctor: you're welcome. bye leo!

Patient: Oh, all the time. I toss and turn. I'll wake up at three in the morning and just start worrying about everything.

Patient: No, no, nothing like that. I love my family too much. I just want to feel like myself again.

Patient: Yes, that sounds okay. Thank you, doctor.

Doctor: Elena Rodriguez, date of birth May 12th, 1982. Patient is a 42-year-old female here for a chief complaint of swollen lymph nodes in the neck. 
Doctor: Hi Ms. Rodriguez, come on in. What brings you in today?
Patient: Hi doctor. Um, I'm just... I'm really worried. I found these lumps in my neck and I'm scared it's, you know, the big C.
Doctor: I understand that can be frightening. Let's take a look and talk about it. When did you first notice these?
Patient: I think it was about two weeks ago. Or maybe... wait, actually, I remember feeling one on the right side about three weeks ago, but it was small. Then last week, the other side got big too.
Doctor: Okay, so about three weeks for the first one, and then the second one appeared more recently. Have you had any other symptoms? Any fevers, or maybe some coughing or a sore throat?
Patient: Yeah, I had a really nasty cold about a month ago. I was just... I was totally wiped out for a week. I still feel a bit tired, but nothing like that. 
Doctor: Any night sweats? Like, waking up and having to change your pajamas because you're so damp?
Patient: No, nothing like that. No.
Doctor: Any unexplained weight loss?
Patient: No, if anything, I've gained a few pounds because I've been so stressed. 
Doctor: I'm sorry to hear that. What's been causing the stress?
Patient: Just... everything. I'm working two jobs right now to keep up with the kids' school stuff, and my childcare is a nightmare. I actually had to move my appointment twice because my sitter cancelled. And honestly, I'm really stressed about the cost. My insurance has this huge deductible this year and I don't know if I can afford a bunch of expensive tests.
Doctor: We will be mindful of that. We'll start with the basics. Let me get a feel of your neck. Go ahead and tilt your head back for me.
Patient: Okay. 
Doctor: Hmm. Okay. Hey Dragon, physical exam: cervical lymphadenopathy present. Right side approximately one centimeter, left side slightly larger, maybe one point five centimeters. Both are mobile, non-fixed, and tender to palpation.
Patient: Does the fact that they hurt mean it's a good thing or a bad thing?
Doctor: Generally, tenderness is actually a reassuring sign. It often suggests that the nodes are reacting to an infection or inflammation rather than something more sinister. Given that you had a bad cold recently, it's very likely these are just reactive nodes—meaning they're doing their job fighting off that virus.
Patient: So I don't need a biopsy or anything?
Doctor: I don't think we are there yet. I want to start with some simple blood work to see what your white blood cell count looks like and maybe check for mononucleosis, just to be thorough.
Patient: Okay. Will that be expensive?
Doctor: A CBC and a mono spot are generally very standard and relatively low-cost. If those come back normal and the lumps don't go down, then we can talk about an ultrasound, but let's not jump ahead.
Patient: Okay, that sounds fair. 
Doctor: Alright, I'll send you to the lab. I want you to keep an eye on them over the next two weeks.
Patient: What should I be looking for?
Doctor: If you notice them getting significantly larger, if they become hard and stop moving when you push them, or if you start having trouble swallowing or breathing, I want you to call the office immediately.
Patient: Okay, I can do that.
Doctor: Great. I'll see you back here in two weeks to review the labs and see if the swelling has gone down.
Patient: Thank you, doctor.

Patient: It's more like... like a fish flopping around in my chest. It doesn't last long, maybe a minute or two, but it makes me nervous. 
Doctor: I see. Have you noticed any shortness of breath, or maybe some swelling in your ankles?
Patient: Now that you mention it, I have been feeling a bit winded. Not like I can't breathe, but like... I'll be carrying the groceries up the stairs to my mom's place and I'm just huffing and puffing way more than I used to.
Doctor: Okay. Any chest pain? Dizziness? Fainting spells?
Patient: No, nothing like that. No pain.
Doctor: Any other things? Any joint pain, fever, or maybe some changes in your bowel habits?
Patient: No, joints are okay. No fever. Everything else seems normal, I think.

Doctor: Good morning, Sarah. It's good to see you. What brings you in today?
Patient: Um, hi doctor. Well, I've been having this... this vaginal discharge for about a week now and it's really starting to worry me.
Doctor: I'm sorry to hear that. Let's talk more about it. Can you describe the discharge for me? What does it look like?
Patient: It's sort of like a thin, grayish-white color. And the thing is, it has this really strong, fishy smell to it. It's just... it's very noticeable, especially after I have sex.
Doctor: Okay. And have you noticed any other symptoms? Any itching, redness, or burning when you go to the bathroom?
Patient: No, no itching. That's the weird part. Usually, if it's a yeast infection, it's like, itching like crazy, right? But this is just the smell and the fluid. I have had some mild pain during intercourse, though.
Doctor: I see. And just to be sure, have you had any fevers, chills, or abdominal pain lately?
Patient: No, nothing like that. I've just been... uh, stressed. I'm working forty-five hours a week at the store right now because we're short-staffed, and my daughter is starting preschool next month, so I've been running around like crazy trying to get her registered.
Doctor: I completely understand. It sounds like you've got a lot on your plate. Speaking of the store, how is the new management treating you?
Patient: Oh, they're okay, I guess. My manager is a bit of a micromanager, but the pay is decent. Though, honestly, I'm a bit worried about the cost of whatever treatment we decide on today. My insurance deductible is really high this year and I'm just... I'm on a tight budget with the kids.
Doctor: We will definitely keep that in mind and look for the most cost-effective options. Now, before we move to the exam, have you tried any over-the-counter creams or medications for this?

Doctor: That was a smart move. Alright, let's go ahead and do a quick pelvic exam. I'll have the nurse bring in the speculum and some swabs.
(A few minutes pass during the examination)
Doctor: Okay, Sarah, I'm just finishing up here. On the exam, I do see that thin, grayish-white discharge. I'm going to perform a quick pH test right here... okay, the pH is elevated, which is common in this situation. I've also taken a swab for a wet mount.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: The wet mount allows me to look at the discharge under a microscope. Actually, let me just pull that up on the screen here... okay, I see a lot of "clue cells." Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells covered in bacteria, which is a hallmark of bacterial vaginosis.
Patient: Bacterial vaginosis? Is that an STI?
Doctor: Not necessarily. While it can be triggered by new sexual partners, it's often just an imbalance of the natural bacteria in the vagina. It's very common and very treatable. Hey Dragon, add a diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis to the chart.
Patient: Oh, thank goodness. I was really anxious that it was something more serious. So, what's the plan?
Doctor: I'm going to prescribe you metronidazole. We can do either a pill or a gel. Given your concerns about cost, the oral tablets are usually very inexpensive. I'll give you a prescription for metronidazole 500 mg tablets, to be taken twice a day for seven days.
Patient: Okay, twice a day for a week. Got it.
Doctor: Now, this is important: you must finish the entire seven-day course, even if the smell goes away after two or three days. If you stop early, the bacteria can come back. Also, I want you to avoid using any douches or scented soaps in that area, as those can make the imbalance worse.
Patient: I'll make sure to finish them. I really don't want to have to come back and pay another co-pay.
Doctor: That's a great motivation! Now, if you find that the symptoms don't improve after finishing the medication, or if you develop a fever, I want you to call my office right away.
Patient: Okay, I can do that.
Doctor: Do you have any other questions for me today?
Patient: No, I think that covers it. Thank you, doctor.
Doctor: You're very welcome. I'll send that prescription to your pharmacy now. Have a great day!

Patient: oh, so i'm not having a stroke?

Patient: thank you, doctor. i feel a lot better just knowing what it is.
Doctor: you're very welcome. just remember, no deep bending or tilting for 24 hours. if you feel a sudden onset of severe headache, fainting, or if you can't speak clearly, i want you to go straight to the emergency room, but otherwise, i'll see you in two weeks.

Patient: oh , i don't know doctor . i'm just ... i'm still feeling so worn out . i feel like i've been hit by a truck and i just can't get my energy back .
Doctor: i'm sorry to hear that . it's been about four weeks since you tested positive , right ?
Patient: yeah , about a month . the fever went away after the first week , but now i'm just ... i'm getting winded so easily . like , just walking from the car to the store , i feel like i can't get enough air .
Doctor: okay . and when you say winded , is it a sharp pain , or just a feeling of shortness of breath ?
Patient: no , no pain . just ... like i'm breathing through a straw . and my head feels all fuzzy . i can't seem to remember where i put my keys or what i was saying halfway through a sentence .
Doctor: that sounds like some brain fog , which we see quite a bit of . um ... are you finding that this is making it hard to get back to your normal routine ?
Patient: it is . i'm trying to get back to my part-time shifts at the pharmacy , but i'm just so tired . and i'm the main one taking care of my mother , she's eighty-two and has dementia , so i'm usually the one lifting her and getting her dressed . i'm just terrified i'm going to drop her because i'm so shaky .
Doctor: i understand that's a lot of pressure . let's talk about some other symptoms . have you noticed any chest pain or your heart going crazy , like skipping beats ?
Patient: no , nothing like that .
Doctor: any swelling in your ankles or legs ?
Patient: no , they look normal .
Doctor: how about your stomach ? any nausea or ... uh ... changes in your bowel movements ?
Patient: no , that's all been fine .
Doctor: and emotionally , how are you holding up ? any new anxiety or trouble sleeping , other than just being tired ?
Patient: well , i'm anxious about my mom , obviously . but i haven't been feeling depressed or anything . i just ... i just want to feel like myself again .
Doctor: that's completely understandable . let's do a quick check. hey dragon , open physical exam template . okay , i'm going to listen to your heart and lungs . just take a deep breath for me .
Patient: [breathes deeply]
Doctor: okay , and again . lungs sound clear bilaterally , no wheezing or crackles . heart is a regular rate and rhythm . hey dragon , record oxygen saturation . okay , your o2 sat is 94 percent on room air . that's a little bit lower than where we'd like it , but not critically low . 
Patient: is that why i feel so winded ?
Doctor: it could be contributing to it . i think we're looking at some post-acute covid syndrome , which people call long covid . the fatigue and the fuzzy head are very common . because of that slight dip in your oxygen and the shortness of breath , i want to get a better look at how your lungs are functioning . hey dragon , order a pulmonary function test . 
Patient: is that a big test ? i can't miss too many more days of work , my manager is already asking when i'm coming back full-time .
Doctor: it's a fairly simple breathing test . we can schedule it for early morning so it doesn't interfere too much with your day . for now , i want you to try a "pacing" approach . don't try to jump right back into everything at once . if you feel yourself getting winded , stop and rest immediately . don't push through it .
Patient: i'm not very good at resting .
Doctor: i know , but pushing too hard can actually make the fatigue worse . so , let's do the pft first , and we'll meet back here in two weeks to go over those results . 
Patient: okay . what if i feel worse before then ?
Doctor: that's important . if you experience any sudden , severe shortness of breath that doesn't go away with rest , or if you develop new chest pain , i want you to go straight to the emergency room . don't wait for a call back from the office . and if you notice your lips or fingernails turning a bluish color , that's also an immediate ER visit .
Patient: okay , er for chest pain or blue nails . i got it .
Doctor: exactly . we'll get that test scheduled for you now .

CHIEF COMPLAINT

COVID-19 follow-up.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Ms. Hargrove is a female patient presenting for a follow-up visit approximately four weeks after a COVID-19 infection. She reports persistent, severe fatigue and describes feeling "like I've been hit by a truck." She endorses dyspnea on exertion, noting she feels "winded" and as if she is "breathing through a straw" during simple activities, such as walking from her car to a store. She also reports cognitive dysfunction, described as a "fuzzy head," including difficulty with memory and word-finding.

Regarding social determinants of health, the patient is a part-time pharmacy employee and expresses concern regarding her manager's expectations for her return to full-time work. She is also the primary caregiver for her 82-year-old mother who has dementia, and she expresses anxiety regarding her ability to safely perform lifting and dressing tasks due to fatigue and shakiness.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Cardiovascular: Negative for chest pain or palpitations. Negative for ankle or leg edema.
• Gastrointestinal: Negative for nausea or changes in bowel movements.
• Psychiatric: Negative for depression. Endorses anxiety related to caregiving responsibilities.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Respiratory
• Auscultation of Lungs: Clear bilaterally; no wheezing or crackles noted.

Cardiovascular
• Auscultation of Heart: Regular rate and rhythm.

RESULTS

Oxygen saturation: 94% on room air.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Post-acute COVID syndrome (Long COVID).
• Medical Reasoning: The patient presents with classic symptoms of post-acute COVID, including persistent fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, and cognitive impairment ("brain fog"), occurring four weeks post-infection.
• Additional Testing: A pulmonary function test (PFT) has been ordered to evaluate lung function due to reported dyspnea and a slightly decreased oxygen saturation.
• Medical Treatment: The patient was advised to utilize a "pacing" strategy, which involves stopping and resting immediately upon the onset of shortness of breath rather than pushing through the activity.

INSTRUCTIONS

The patient was instructed to go immediately to the emergency room if she experiences:
1. Sudden, severe shortness of breath that does not resolve with rest.
2. New onset of chest pain.
3. Cyanosis (bluish color) of the lips or fingernails.

The patient is scheduled to follow up in two weeks to review PFT results.

Doctor: hi mrs. harris, it's good to see you. i see you're coming in today for a skin rash. can you tell me a bit more about what's going on?
Patient: oh doctor, it's just... it's awful. i'm just itching like crazy. it's all over my arms and my stomach, and i just can't stop scratching it. i'm worried it's something... you know, something bad.
Doctor: i understand. when did you first notice this starting?
Patient: well, it was maybe three days ago. i was out in my garden, you know, pulling weeds and trying to get the tomatoes in before the rain. and then by that evening, i started getting these little red bumps. 
Doctor: okay, and have you used any new soaps, lotions, or detergents recently?
Patient: no, nothing new. i've used the same soap for twenty years. though, i did try a new kind of fertilizer for the roses, but i wore my gloves. mostly. i think i might have touched a bit of it with my bare hands though.
Doctor: okay, so you might have had some direct contact. have you ever had anything like this happen before?
Patient: well, let's see. oh! about ten years ago, i think it was a summer in ohio, i got something similar after a hiking trip, but that was more like blisters. this is more... just bumpy and red.
Doctor: okay, so a similar but slightly different reaction in the past. i'm sorry to interrupt, but i want to make sure we cover a few things. are you feeling okay otherwise? any fever, chills, or maybe some joint pain?
Patient: no fever. my knees always hurt, but that's just because i'm sixty-two and i spend all day chasing my grandkids around. they're just little bundles of energy, you know? my oldest grandson is starting kindergarten this fall and he's so nervous, he's been staying with me more often, and i've just been trying to make sure he feels okay about it...
Doctor: that's very sweet of you to support him. now, just to be sure, any shortness of breath or swelling in your face or throat?
Patient: no, nothing like that. just the itching. it's just driving me crazy.
Doctor: alright, let's take a look at that rash. if you could just lift up your shirt and roll up your sleeves for me. 
Patient: okay, here you go.
Doctor: okay, i'm seeing some erythema—that's the redness—and some small papules, which are those little bumps, across your bilateral forearms and the upper part of your abdomen. it does look quite inflamed. does it hurt when i press here, or is it just itchy?
Patient: oh, it's just itchy. it doesn't really hurt.
Doctor: okay. no blistering, no open sores. alright, you can get dressed. 
Patient: thank you. so, what is it? am i going to be okay?
Doctor: i'm fairly confident this is contact dermatitis. basically, your skin had a reaction to something you touched in the garden—likely that fertilizer or perhaps some poison ivy you didn't see. it's not dangerous, but it is certainly uncomfortable. 
Patient: oh, thank goodness. i was worried it was some kind of allergy that was going to get worse.
Doctor: we can get it under control. here is the plan. i'm going to prescribe a topical steroid cream to bring down the inflammation and an oral antihistamine for the itching. 
Patient: um, is the cream expensive? i'm on a very tight fixed income with my pension, and i've been spending so much on the kids' school supplies lately. i can't really afford anything fancy.
Doctor: i completely understand. i'll prescribe a generic hydrocortisone cream and a generic diphenhydramine. those are very affordable and available at any pharmacy. hey dragon, order hydrocortisone 2.5 percent cream and diphenhydramine 25 milligrams. 
Patient: thank you, doctor. i appreciate that.
Doctor: you're welcome. now, for the instructions. i want you to apply the hydrocortisone cream to the affected areas twice a day—once in the morning and once at night. for the diphenhydramine, you can take one tablet every six hours as needed for the itching, but just be aware that it can make you sleepy, so don't take it right before you have to drive the kids around.
Patient: okay, twice a day for the cream, and the pills every six hours if i'm itchy. got it.
Doctor: exactly. now, this is important: if you notice any swelling of your lips, tongue, or throat, or if you start having any trouble breathing, i want you to go to the emergency room immediately or call 911. that would be a sign of a more severe allergic reaction. 
Patient: oh dear, i'll keep a close eye on that. 
Doctor: i'd also like you to call my office and let me know if the rash doesn't start to improve in three to four days, or if you see any yellow crusting or pus, which could mean it's getting infected. 
Patient: alright, i can do that.
Doctor: great. i'll see you back here in one week just to make sure everything is clearing up.
Patient: sounds good. thank you again.
Doctor: you're welcome. take care.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Skin rash.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Mrs. Harris is a 62-year-old female who presents with an itchy skin rash. The patient reports that the symptoms began approximately three days ago after gardening. She notes the presence of red bumps on her arms and stomach. She mentions that she may have had direct skin contact with a new rose fertilizer. The patient recalls a similar episode approximately 10 years ago following a hiking trip, although she describes that previous episode as having blisters. 

The patient is a caregiver for her grandchildren and reports being on a tight fixed income due to her pension, expressing concern regarding the cost of medications.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

• Constitutional: Denies fever and chills.
• Musculoskeletal: Reports chronic knee pain.
• Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.
• Integumentary: Endorses pruritus and rash on arms and abdomen.
• Neurological: Denies swelling of the face or throat.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

• Integumentary: Examination of the bilateral forearms and upper abdomen reveals erythema and small papules. No blistering or open sores noted. Area is tender to palpation only for pruritus, not pain.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

Contact dermatitis.
• Medical Reasoning: The timing of the rash following gardening and the clinical appearance of erythematous papules suggest a contact reaction to an environmental irritant or allergen (e.g., fertilizer or poison ivy).
• Medical Treatment: 
  1. Hydrocortisone 2.5% cream: Apply to affected areas twice daily (morning and night).
  2. Diphenhydramine 25 mg: One tablet every six hours as needed for pruritus.

INSTRUCTIONS

The patient was instructed to seek immediate emergency care (ER or 911) if she experiences swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, or any difficulty breathing. The patient was advised to call the office if the rash does not improve in 3-4 days or if signs of infection develop, such as yellow crusting or pus. The patient was cautioned that diphenhydramine may cause drowsiness and should be used carefully when driving.

Follow up in one week to ensure resolution of symptoms.

Doctor: We'll use your insurance, and I'll make sure we only do what's necessary. I'm going to start by performing an ear irrigation to clear the wax. Then, I want to send you to our audiologist for a full hearing test.
Patient: Okay, that sounds fair. My daughter is waiting in the car, so as long as it doesn't take all day, I'm good.
Doctor: It shouldn't take long. Hey Dragon, order a comprehensive audiometry panel for mr. penhaligon. 
Doctor: All right, arthur. We'll get you cleaned up, and then you'll head over to the hearing booth. If it turns out you have permanent loss from the mill, we can talk about hearing aids, but let's see the results first.
Patient: Sounds like a plan. Thank you, doctor.
Doctor: You're welcome. Let's get started with that irrigation.
